title_en: Tang v. Li and Tang B — dispute over statutory inheritance
ruling_gist_en: An agreement on the division of property during marriage between a husband and wife is a contract by which the parties agree on the matrimonial property regime to be adopted. It is the result of the internal distribution of family property through mutual agreement. In cases where the interests of third parties outside the marriage and family are not involved, the true intention of the husband and wife should be respected, and the agreement on the division of property during marriage should be performed. The factual property right holder should be given priority protection, and property registration should not be used as the sole basis for determining the ownership of real property.

full_text_en:
Tang B v. Li and Tang C — dispute over statutory inheritance

Ruling Summary

A marital property division agreement reached between a husband and wife is an agreement by which both parties, through entering into a contract, stipulate the type of matrimonial property regime to be adopted. It is the result of mutual negotiation and internal distribution of family property. Where no interests of third parties outside the family are involved, the true expression of intent between the husband and wife should be respected, the agreement should be performed in accordance with the marital property division agreement reached by both parties, and preference should be given to protecting the factual property right holder; the property registration should not be used as the sole basis for determining the ownership of immovable property.

Plaintiff: Tang B, female, 28 years old, residing at Qixingyuan, Shijingshan District, Beijing.

Defendant: Li, female, 48 years old, residing at Jinxing Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing.

Defendant: Tang C, male, 14 years old, residing at Jinxing Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Li (mother of Tang C), female, 48 years old, residing at Jinxing Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing.

The plaintiff, Tang B, filed a lawsuit with the Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing against the defendants, Li and Tang C, concerning a dispute over statutory inheritance.

The plaintiff, Tang B, alleged: Tang A died suddenly on September 16, 2011, while on a business trip away from home, and left no will. Among the property registered in his name were multiple properties, including a certain unit at Fortune Center, No. 23, East Third Ring North Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing (hereinafter referred to as the Fortune Center property), bank deposits, a car, etc. The heirs of Tang A are his spouse, Li, and his children, Tang B and Tang C. The plaintiff now petitions the court for an order that the entire estate of Tang A be jointly inherited by Tang B, Tang C, and Li in accordance with the law.

The defendants, Li and Tang C, argued: They acknowledged that Li, Tang B, and Tang C are all heirs of Tang A and may take part in the inheritance. However, the Fortune Center property registered in Tang A's name is not Tang A's property and should not be inherited as part of his estate. Although the property was purchased in Tang A's name and a loan was taken from Bank of China, according to the "Separation Agreement" signed by Tang A and Li, the Fortune Center property belongs to Li as her personal property. The reason why the registration was not changed to Li's name was that the loan had not yet been fully repaid. This agreement was not premised on divorce; it constituted an arrangement between the parties regarding their post-marital joint property. Before Tang A's death, neither party had repudiated this agreement. Therefore, the agreement is valid, the Fortune Center property is Li's personal property, and it does not form part of Tang A's estate. The defendants agreed that the other property in Tang A's name may be divided and inherited in accordance with the law.

The Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing found the following facts at first instance:

Tang A and the defendant Li were husband and wife, and they had a son, Tang C. Tang A also had a daughter, Tang B, from a previous marriage; after the divorce, Tang B was raised by her mother. Tang A's parents had both predeceased him. Tang A died suddenly of illness on September 16, 2011, while on a business trip away from home, leaving no will.

On October 2, 2010, Tang A and the defendant Li signed a "Separation Agreement," which provided: "The feelings between Tang A and Li have broken down. To avoid hurting our son's heart, we have decided to separate. Our property is divided as follows: The properties at Fortune Center and Huigu Genyuan now belong to Li. Li may dispose of these properties in any manner, and Tang A shall not obstruct or object and is obligated to assist in handling relevant matters. The properties at Huzhong Zhongjie and Huajia Di belong to Tang A. Tang A may dispose of these properties in any manner, and Li shall not obstruct or object and is obligated to assist in handling relevant matters. Our son Tang C belongs to Li. Tang A shall bear the responsibilities of custody, maintenance, and education. Li shall pay monthly living expenses of 5,000 yuan. The parties have adopted the method of 'separating but not leaving home' to resolve the problem of broken feelings. To better achieve the effect, neither party shall interfere in the other's private life or personal affairs." On November 28, 2012, Beijing Minsheng Forensic Science Judicial Appraisal Institute issued a judicial appraisal opinion concluding that the signature of Tang A on the "Separation Agreement" was authentic.

Regarding the Fortune Center property, on December 16, 2002, Tang A, as the purchaser, signed a "Commercial Housing Sales Contract" with Beijing Xiangjiang Xingli Real Estate Development Co., Ltd., agreeing to purchase the Fortune Center property developed by Beijing Xiangjiang Xingli Real Estate Development Co., Ltd., for a total price of 1,579,796 yuan. During the trial, the plaintiff Tang B and the defendants Tang C and Li all confirmed that as of the date of Tang A's death, the property remained registered in Tang A's name and that an outstanding bank loan of 877,125.88 yuan remained unpaid. In addition, Li and Tang A jointly owned two other properties, a car, and bank deposits.

The issue in dispute at first instance was: How to determine the scope of Tang A's estate.

The Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing held at first instance:

The plaintiff Tang B and the defendant Tang C, as children of the decedent Tang A, and the defendant Li, as the spouse of the decedent Tang A, are all first-order statutory heirs and should share Tang A's estate equally. In this case, it is necessary to define which property constitutes Tang A's estate. With respect to the Fortune Center property, although Tang A and Li agreed in the "Separation Agreement" that the property would belong to Li, the property remained registered in Tang A's name up to the time of his death. Therefore, the agreement was not actually performed, and accordingly, based on the principle of registration for real property rights, it should be determined that the property is joint property of Tang A and Li. The value of the property should be determined by subtracting the outstanding loan amount at the time of Tang A's death from the amount determined by the appraisal report; half of that value is Li's share of the joint property, and the other half is Tang A's estate. The portion of Tang A's estate should be divided equally into three shares, to be shared equally by Li, Tang C, and Tang B. Considering that Tang C is a minor and Tang B seeks a monetary compensation, the court ordered that the property be awarded to Li, that Li pay Tang B monetary compensation, and that Li repay the remaining loan on the property. As for the other properties, vehicles, and bank deposits in Tang A's name, the court divided them in accordance with the relevant provisions on statutory inheritance.

In summary, the Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing, pursuant to Articles 2, 3, 5, 10, and 13 of the Inheritance Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on April 8, 2014:

1. The Beijing Hyundai sedan with license plate number京KN××××, part of the estate of the decedent Tang A, is inherited by the defendant Li and belongs to the defendant Li. The defendant Li shall pay the plaintiff Tang B monetary compensation of 16,666.67 yuan within ten days from the effective date of this judgment.

2. The property at Huzhong Zhongjie, Chaoyang District, Beijing, part of the estate of the decedent Tang A, belongs to the defendant Li. The defendant Li shall pay the plaintiff Tang B monetary compensation of 1,800,000 yuan within ten days from the effective date of this judgment.

3. The property at Fortune Center, No. 23, East Third Ring North Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing, part of the estate of the decedent Tang A, belongs to the defendant Li, and Li shall repay the remaining loan. The defendant Li shall pay the plaintiff Tang B monetary compensation of 885,180.69 yuan within ten days from the effective date of this judgment.

4. The defendant Li shall pay the plaintiff Tang B a one-time funeral subsidy of 18,366.67 yuan from the estate of the decedent Tang A within ten days from the effective date of this judgment.

5. The defendant Li shall pay the plaintiff Tang B a living allowance of 5,366.67 yuan for family members issued by the labor union from the estate of the decedent Tang A within ten days from the effective date of this judgment.

6. The other claims of the plaintiff Tang B are dismissed.

Li and Tang C, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing Third Intermediate People's Court, arguing: The "Separation Agreement" signed by Tang A and Li should be characterized as a marital property division agreement. The Fortune Center property, regardless of in whose name it was registered, should have its ownership determined by the effective marital property agreement between Tang A and Li. They requested that the appellate court set aside the original judgment and instead rule that the Fortune Center property is Li's personal property and not part of Tang A's estate.

The appellee Tang B argued: The first-instance court found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly; she requested that the appellate court render a judgment in accordance with the law.

Upon appeal, the Beijing Third Intermediate People's Court confirmed the facts found at first instance.

The issue in dispute on appeal was: The ownership of the Fortune Center property and whether it should be inherited as part of Tang A's estate.

The Beijing Third Intermediate People's Court held on appeal:

Resolving this issue turns on clarifying the following three sub-issues:

First, the legal nature of the "Separation Agreement" signed by Tang A and the appellant Li on October 2, 2010.

The appellants Li and Tang C argued that the agreement is a marital property division agreement, constituting a stipulation between Tang A and Li concerning the ownership of property acquired during their marriage. This stipulation is lawful and valid and binding on both parties. Tang B argued that the agreement is a divorce property division agreement reached for the purpose of divorce and that, since the parties did not divorce, the agreement has no legal effect. The court held that the "Separation Agreement" signed by Tang A and Li in this case is a marital property division agreement, not a divorce property division agreement. The reasons are as follows:

First, from the content of the "Separation Agreement," Tang A and the appellant Li acknowledged that their feelings had broken down but expressly agreed to adopt the method of "separating but not leaving home" to resolve the problem of broken feelings so as to avoid hurting their son's heart. The parties, while still in the marital relationship, chose separation as a solution and divided their joint property; they did not reach a property division agreement for the purpose of divorce. Second, from the perspective of textual interpretation, the "Separation Agreement" signed by the two parties does not mention "divorce" at all; obviously, it was not intended to divide joint property for divorce. On the contrary, the parties expressly used the terms "separation" and "separating but not leaving home" in the agreement, thereby using the agreement to avoid the occurrence of the legal fact of divorce. Third, Article 19(1) of the Marriage Law clearly provides for the marital property agreement system: "Husband and wife may agree that the property acquired during the marriage and the pre-marital property shall be owned separately, jointly, or partly separately and partly jointly. Such agreement shall be in writing. Where there is no agreement or the agreement is unclear, the provisions of Articles 17 and 18 of this Law shall apply." In the "Separation Agreement" involved in this case, Tang A and Li jointly stated that they would "cut the property as follows." This stipulation constitutes a division of property acquired during the marriage by Tang A and Li, not for the purpose of divorce, and should be characterized as a marital property division agreement, i.e., an agreement by which both parties, through entering into a contract, stipulated the type of matrimonial property regime to be adopted.

Second, whether the relevant legal provisions of the Property Law or the Marriage Law should apply preferentially in this case.

The appellants Li and Tang C argued that Article 19 of the Marriage Law should apply: as long as the husband and wife have made a written agreement on property division, it becomes legally effective without the need for registration of title transfer. The appellee Tang B argued that Article 9 of the Property Law should apply in this case: changes in the ownership of immovable property are not legally effective without registration. The court held that this issue requires first clarifying the interface and application of the Property Law and the Marriage Law when adjusting property relations within the realm of marriage and family. For this case, the relevant provisions of the Marriage Law should be applied preferentially. The reasons are as follows:

In the field of property rights, legal subjects establish relationships due to property. The Property Law, as a fundamental law regulating property relations between equal subjects arising from the ownership and use of property, focuses on the relationship between the subject and the property, and its legislative purpose is to protect transaction security to promote efficient use of resources. In contrast, the Marriage Law, as a law of status, aims to regulate the personal and property relations between husband and wife. Property relations under the Marriage Law are attached to personal relations and are limited to rights and obligations arising from status between persons of the opposite sex or among family members. They do not reflect direct economic purposes but rather highlight the requirements of family life and family functions. Accordingly, the provisions of the Marriage Law concerning special personal or property relations between husband and wife, parent and child, etc., are not created or exist for utilitarian purposes but carry a flavor of "public law" and overtones of social security and institutional welfare, directly incorporating the value orientations of protecting the "weak" and "altruism" into considerations of rights and obligations.

Therefore, the group characteristics of the marriage and family determine that the Marriage Law cannot be entirely individual-oriented; it must take into account the interests of the husband-wife community and the family community, which differs from the individual-oriented approach of the Property Law. In adjusting the field of husband-wife property relations, the Property Law should exercise restraint and respect the scope of application and regulatory function of the Marriage Law. In particular, agreements between husband and wife concerning specific property regimes should not be overly regulated by the Property Law but should be normatively evaluated by the Marriage Law. In this case, the division of the Fortune Center property in the agreement signed by Tang A and the appellant Li is an internal arrangement of property between husband and wife that does not involve external relations. Therefore, the relevant provisions of the Marriage Law should be applied preferentially and primarily, while the relevant legal provisions of the Property Law, which regulate property relations between general subjects, should serve as a supplement.

Third, whether the principle of public summons of immovable property registration under the Property Law has mandatory applicability in the realm of husband-wife property.

The appellants Li and Tang C argued that a marital property division agreement concerns only the attribution of property between husband and wife, which can be determined by the agreement itself without requiring public summons as a condition for the change of property rights. The appellee Tang B argued that the owner of the Fortune Center property was Tang A and that even if Tang A and Li had agreed that the property would belong to Li, since the registration of title was not changed, the change of property rights did not occur, and the property should still be included in Tang A's estate. The court held that the "Separation Agreement" signed by Tang A and Li had already determined that the Fortune Center property belongs exclusively to Li. Although the property remained registered in Tang A's name, this does not affect the validity of the internal disposition between the parties. The reasons are as follows:

The Property Law adopts registration as the statutory method of public summons for changes in real property rights, conferring public trust on registration, with the aim of clarifying the attribution of property rights, protecting transaction security and transaction order, and improving transaction efficiency. However, in practice, due to exceptions provided by law, erroneous registration, changes in the validity of legal acts, the true reservation of intent of the parties, and compliance with trade customs, there exist a large number of factual property rights that lack the external form of registration but should, according to law, equity, and reason, be granted legal protection. Articles 28 to 30 of the Property Law also provide illustrative provisions on changes in property rights not based on legal acts, enumerating situations where changes in property rights may occur directly without the need for public summons. Of course, these illustrative provisions do not exhaust all situations where changes in property rights occur not based on legal acts; the relevant situations provided for in the Marriage Law and its judicial interpretations should also be included.

In the realm of husband-wife property, there are many cases where, after marriage, one spouse signs a property purchase contract and registers the property in that spouse's name. However, in practice, as long as there is no separate agreement between the husband and wife, both spouses jointly own property acquired after marriage. This is based on the statutory property regime under the Marriage Law, not on a legal act between the parties. Because marriage, as an objective fact, already has the characteristic of public summons and does not require additional public summons. The agreed property regime between husband and wife is a clear stipulation made by both spouses in writing, on the basis of equality, voluntariness, and true expression of intent, concerning the attribution of jointly owned property acquired after marriage. Such a stipulation fully reflects the true will of the spouses and is the result of party autonomy, which should be respected and protected by law. Therefore, in principle, it should also be included within the scope of changes in property rights that may occur directly without a legal act. Consequently, when a dispute arises over the attribution of immovable property jointly acquired by husband and wife after marriage, a comprehensive determination should be made based on factors such as whether the causal act causing the change in immovable property rights is valid and whether third-party interests are involved. It is inappropriate to use the property registration as the sole basis for determining the ownership of immovable property. As long as there is sufficient evidence to establish the ownership status of the immovable property and no third-party interests are involved, the true expression of intent between husband and wife should be respected, the marital property division agreement reached by both parties should be performed, and preference should be given to protecting the factual property right holder. It should be noted that the "third party" referred to here is mainly relative to the outside of the marriage and family relationship. For example, if the husband-wife property involves disposing of property rights to third parties outside the family, the Property Law and other relevant laws regulating property relations between general subjects should apply. However, for property issues within the husband-wife family relationship, the relevant provisions of the Marriage Law should be applied preferentially.

In this case, the "Separation Agreement" provided: "The Fortune Center property belongs to Li. Li may dispose of this property in any manner, and Tang A shall not obstruct or object and is obligated to assist in handling relevant matters." This agreement is an internal arrangement between Tang A and the appellant Li based on their marital relationship. It is the result of the two parties, on the basis of equality and voluntariness, negotiating and allocating family property between themselves. It does not involve the interests of third parties outside the marriage and family. It possesses the nature of a civil contract and is binding on both parties. The Fortune Center property has not entered market circulation for transaction, and determining its ownership does not involve transaction order or circulation security. Therefore, although Tang B raised objections to the validity of this agreement in this case, as a child of Tang A, she is not a "third party" within the meaning of the Property Law. Consequently, although the Fortune Center property was registered in Tang A's name, and the parties did not complete the registration of title transfer due to the outstanding loan, the principle of immovable property registration under the Property Law should not affect the validity of the marital property division agreement regarding the attribution of the property. Moreover, considering that Tang A and Li had, in accordance with the "Separation Agreement," respectively occupied, used, and managed the relevant properties, the Fortune Center property should be recognized as Li's personal property and not part of Tang A's estate for statutory inheritance. The first-instance court, based on the principle of registration for real property rights, determined that the Fortune Center property was joint property of Tang A and Li; this was inappropriate and should be corrected.

Accordingly, the Beijing Third Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 9 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 19 of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 2, 3, 5, 10, and 13 of the Inheritance Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 170(1)(ii) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on August 25, 2014:

1. Items 1, 2, 4, and 5 of the civil judgment (2013) Chaomin Chuzi No. 30975 of the Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing are affirmed.

2. Item 6 of the civil judgment (2013) Chaomin Chuzi No. 30975 of the Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing is set aside.

3. Item 3 of the main text of the civil judgment (2013) Chaomin Chuzi No. 30975 of the Chaoyang District People's Court of Beijing is changed to: The property at Fortune Center, No. 23, East Third Ring North Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing, belongs to Li, and Li shall repay the remaining loan.

4. The other claims of Tang B are dismissed.

This judgment is final.
